title: I wanted to make a robot boxing game, but the AI couldn't draw humanoid robots fighting. It ended up as a warehouse game about cargo robots
author: office-canard
selftext:
FREIGHT FRIGHT has nothing to do with freight in its DNA. It started as a robot boxing match.



I'd seen footage out of China of humanoid robots boxing each other, and I wanted to make a game where you're the builder and the cornerman, not the fighter in the ring. Then I hit a wall: the AI couldn't draw a humanoid robot fighting. Not a single believable moving robot. So I tried BattleBots instead, wedge-and-wheels machines slamming into each other. That, an AI can draw.



Then the camera question took over the whole project. I built a 3D version in three.js with Claude, and it came out better than I expected. From there my interest moved from the game to the tool. I started hunting for a setting that would put 3D to better use.



The first thing that came to mind was I.Q., the old PlayStation puzzler where cubes roll toward you across a grid. Then the cubes started looking like cardboard boxes. That's the nightmare you have in an Amazon warehouse.



Years ago, as a writer, I covered AMRs, the swarms of AI-driven warehouse robots. So I made one the hero. You're an AMR, and you team up with an AGV, an automated guided vehicle, that hauls your cargo to the dock.



And after all that, I threw the 3D away. This kind of fun plays better on a flat map, like Pac-Man or Bomberman. The tool that started the whole project disappeared the moment the game got better without it.



How it plays:



\- You're the blue AMR. Your green AGV partner holds only five parcels.

\- Hit SEND and the AGV runs the load to the dock and comes back. While it's gone, you can't collect anything.

\- So the real choice isn't which parcel to grab. It's when to send. Wait for a full load, or send early and eat the downtime.

\- Meanwhile, red rogue AMRs tear around the floor stealing cargo. ZAP them to knock it loose and take it back.

\- Get 24 parcels onto the rocket before time runs out.



How AI fit in: Claude wrote the code, first the 3D version in three.js and then the flat-map version that shipped. The art came from image AI, which is why the robot boxing idea died: it could draw BattleBots, but not a humanoid robot throwing a punch.



The brawl survived in the end, just in a different shape. It started as robots punching each other and ended as you fighting AI robots over cargo.
